opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is that compute is one of the main inputs to everything we do. When you look at how AI progress has happened over the last several years, a huge fraction of it has come from scaling, from training larger models on more data with more compute. If you take that seriously, then how efficiently you can use compute isn't a back-office concern. It directly shapes what models you can train, how quickly you can learn things, and whether you're anywhere near the frontier at all.

For Anthropic specifically, our strategy depends on being at the frontier. A lot of the safety research we care about, like understanding how models behave, studying alignment techniques, and doing interpretability on systems that actually resemble the most capable ones, only works if you have access to frontier-scale models. If we're a generation or two behind, our research may not tell us much about the systems that matter. And our ability to influence norms in the industry, or show that you can be safety-focused and still build useful, competitive products, depends on staying at that level too.

Infrastructure is where a lot of that gets won or lost. You can buy or rent a lot of chips, but turning that hardware into useful training runs is really hard. You have to get thousands of accelerators working together reliably, deal with hardware failures constantly, make sure your networking isn't the bottleneck, and design your parallelism strategy so you're getting high utilization. The difference between a well-designed system and a mediocre one can easily be a big multiplier in effective compute. That's like getting a much larger budget for free.

There's also a speed-of-iteration piece. Research is fundamentally about running experiments and learning from them. If your infrastructure is flaky, or researchers have to wait a long time to get results, or it's painful to launch a job, that slows everything down. Good infrastructure means people spend their time thinking about the science rather than fighting the tooling.

And then from a safety and security perspective, the way you design these systems matters too. As models get more capable, things like protecting model weights and having good controls over how training and deployment happen become more important. Building that in from the start is much easier than retrofitting it.

So I don't really think of infrastructure as separate from the mission. It's a big part of what makes the rest of the work possible.

r001.rationale: It says well-designed infrastructure can turn the same hardware into a much larger amount of effective compute through reliability, networking, and high utilization.

r002.rationale: It describes infrastructure improving effective compute, but does not connect that benefit to the cost characteristics of Anthropic’s particular workloads.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that compute is the thing that everything else is downstream of. At Anthropic, the amount of compute you have access to — and, maybe more importantly, how efficiently you can actually use it — basically sets the ceiling on what kind of models you can train and how fast you can iterate on research.

And I think people sometimes imagine that the hard part is just buying the chips. Like, you go get a bunch of GPUs or TPUs and then you're done. But in practice, the gap between "we have X chips" and "we're actually getting X chips' worth of useful training out of them" is enormous. You've got thousands of accelerators that need to talk to each other constantly, you've got hardware failures happening on a regular basis at that scale, you've got networking bottlenecks, storage bottlenecks, all these places where you can lose 20 or 30 or 50 percent of your effective capacity if you haven't designed things carefully. So a lot of the work is really about closing that gap.

The other piece is that our workloads are pretty unusual compared to what a lot of general-purpose infrastructure was built for. A large training run is one enormous, tightly coupled job that has to run for weeks or months without falling over. That's just a very different problem from serving a web app, where you can have lots of small independent requests and if one fails you retry it. So we end up having to think carefully about things like checkpointing, fault tolerance, how you shard a model across many chips, how you keep the whole system healthy over a long period of time.

And then I'd add a safety angle to it as well, which is something I care about a lot. Part of the reason Anthropic exists is the belief that it matters who's at the frontier of this technology. If we want to be in a position to do the safety research we think is important, and to have influence over how these systems get developed and deployed, we need to actually be able to train frontier models. That's not possible without really good infrastructure. So it's not glamorous work in some ways, but I genuinely think of it as one of the load-bearing pieces of the whole mission.

r001.rationale: It explains that efficiently coordinating thousands of accelerators turns more of Anthropic’s chips into useful training capacity, increasing effective compute.

r002.rationale: It says Anthropic’s workloads have unusual technical requirements and that tailored infrastructure improves utilization, but does not connect that design to the workloads’ cost characteristics.

astra-6.text:
Compute infrastructure is critical because it determines how quickly we can run experiments and learn from them. You can have a promising research idea, but if testing it takes too long, or the system keeps failing, that really limits the progress you can make.

And that matters for safety research as well as for building more capable models. We need to be able to evaluate models, understand their behavior, and test ways of making them more reliable. All of that requires compute. So I see infrastructure as a way of making the whole research organization more effective: giving researchers dependable tools and a faster path from an idea to evidence about whether it works.

r001.rationale: The response says infrastructure provides compute and speeds research, but does not identify combining large amounts of compute as a multiplier on Anthropic’s effective compute capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of AI research is experimental. You have an idea, you run an experiment, and you use the result to decide what to try next. So the infrastructure determines both how many experiments researchers can run and how quickly they can learn from them.

For a company like Anthropic, that matters for capabilities research, but also for safety research: understanding how models behave, evaluating them, and testing ways to make them more reliable. Those workloads need compute that’s available, efficient, and easy for researchers to use.

So I see infrastructure as a multiplier on the research team. If you can reduce the time people spend waiting for a run or debugging an infrastructure problem, you give them more time to work on the actual scientific questions.

r001.rationale: The response calls infrastructure a multiplier on the research team and says it enables more experiments, but does not identify using large amounts of compute together as the multiplier on effective compute capacity.
